title: How the U.S. Postal Service Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the United States Postal Service (USPS): its finances and projected cash shortfall in October 2013, the proposed end of Saturday letter delivery, and the 2006 congressional mandate to prepay retiree benefits. They cover the history of American mail from the 1639 Boston tavern post, Richard Fairbanks' tavern, William Penn's post office, Thomas Neil's grant, Benjamin Franklin as first Postmaster General, the Pony Express and Overland Mail, the 1971 reorganization into the USPS, the "going postal" phenomenon, ZIP codes and automated sorting, how a letter moves through processing, addressing guidelines, media mail, package delivery competition with UPS and FedEx, postal rate setting, PO boxes and mailbox installation rules, and future plans such as federal email addresses, prescription delivery and clothing line. The episode closes with a listener mail correction about subliminal messages in 1950s films and a food drive mention.

segments.title: Opening banter and USPS solvency warning
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, then introduce the topic of the US Postal Service and its projected cash shortfall in October 2013.

segments.title: Retiree benefit prepayment and Saturday delivery cut
segments.summary: The USPS lost large sums largely due to required prepayment of future retiree benefits mandated in 2006. Proposed cut to Saturday letter delivery, Senate and House action, and the USPS argument that its 1981 mandate is not in the stopgap budget. Package and medicine delivery would continue on Saturdays.

segments.title: Mail volume, revenue, and employee decline
segments.summary: Mail volume peaked around 2006 and has declined since; employee count dropped from about 700,000 to about 580,000; postal revenue remains large from stamps but the service still loses money.

segments.title: Colonial posts and early American postal history
segments.summary: Early postal service begins with a 1639 official drop at Richard Fairbanks' tavern in Boston, William Penn's Pennsylvania post office in 1683, and Thomas Neil's 1691 grant. The Continental Congress founded its own post office in 1774 and Benjamin Franklin became the first Postmaster General.

segments.title: Westward mail routes and the Pony Express
segments.summary: During the California Gold Rush, mail went by steamship around Florida, Caribbean, and Panama, taking three to four weeks. The Overland Mail Company used the southern and central routes. The Pony Express, run by a rival company, proved the central route could be used year round, but the government split the contract. The telegraph ended the Pony Express.

segments.title: 1971 reorganization and universal delivery mandate
segments.summary: The Post Office Department became the independent United States Postal Service in 1971, retaining a monopoly on letter delivery and a mandate for universal delivery to every address, including remote areas such as a Grand Canyon donkey mail route.

segments.title: Going postal and workplace shootings
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the origin of the phrase going postal, tied to a series of workplace shootings by postal workers starting in 1986, and a documentary about them. They note retail has a higher homicide rate.

segments.title: ZIP codes and automated sorting
segments.summary: ZIP codes were introduced in 1963 and made mandatory later, as the first step to automation; ZIP stands for Zone Improvement Plan. The digits are explained from state to local delivery, and plus-four codes add specificity.

segments.title: How a letter moves through processing and addressing tips
segments.summary: A letter is picked up, taken to a processing plant, faced and oriented, postmarked, barcoded, and read by optical scanners, with video coding for hard-to-read handwriting. Guidelines include legible addresses, return address in the upper left, and avoiding periods and commas. Media mail is a cheap option for books and DVDs.

segments.title: Package competition, rates, PO boxes, and mailbox rules
segments.summary: The USPS competes with UPS and FedEx for packages, and it delivers the last mile for them. Postal rates are hard to change due to bureaucracy. Mailbox height and setback guidelines are described, along with PO boxes.

segments.title: Future plans, food drive, and sign-off
segments.summary: Future USPS plans include federal email addresses, prescription delivery, and a rain heat or snow clothing line; the Herodotus-derived creed is discussed. The food drive is mentioned and the hosts close with contact information. Listener mail about subliminal messages is also mentioned.
